sections.name: Update
paragraphs: An additional wind advisory has been issued for the City and Borough of Sitka, joining Ketchikan, Prince of Wales Island and Annette Island. These advisories remain in effect through this afternoon (Sitka remains through this evening). Expecting east to southeast winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 45 mph following this current frontal passage. Marine winds increasing across the southern panhandle with Clarence Strait and the coastal zones currently in a Gale Warning through this evening.
Also an update to the aviation discussion section below, following the 18Z TAF package issuance...

sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT ...459 AM AKST Tue Nov 24 2026

- As a front exits the panhandle Tuesday morning, a second front begins to move northward into the area. This next front will be very similar to the previous system once again increasing winds and precipitation chances.
- A wind advisory continues into Tuesday afternoon for Prince of Wales Island, Ketchikan and Annette Island for gusts around 40 mph.
- Multiple rounds of rain and wind are likely this week with the possibility of some drier and cooler weather this weekend.

SHORT TERM.../Through Wednesday night/ The first of a series of weather fronts that will affect the panhandle through the week is moving through the northern panhandle this morning. Winds both ahead and along the front have lightened up overnight with mainly around 25 kt winds being observed in Stephens Passage, Cross Sound, and Lynn Canal. Precipitation has been on the lighter side as well with the rain/snow line running through Icy Strait and the middle of Juneau this morning. Any snow accumulations have been light with less then 1 inch observed most places.

The front across the north is expected to continue to weaken and pull away to the NW through Tue morning taking what is left of its wind and precip with it. Focus then shifts to a new low that will be riding up the outer coast this morning. The strength of this feature is relatively new with gale force winds accompanying it just about all the way to just south of Yakutat for the near shore waters of the gulf by Tuesday evening. Inland expect more gusty winds and precip as the feature moves north. Southern Panhandle will get another round of wind gusts of 40+ mph mainly around late morning. Most inner channels of the north half of the panhandle will likely stay with north to NE winds into Tuesday night. Precip will mostly be rain this time around with any low elevation snow only expected to show up from northern Lynn northward. Any snow accumulation is again expected to be light with the most accumulation likely on the Haines Highway with up to 2 inches of snow expected Tuesday night.

Active weather continues into Wednesday night with overall southerly onshore flow and embedded troughs in the flow bringing continued precip and some gusty winds. At least two more waves are possible with one arriving late Tuesday night, and a second coming Wednesday night. Neither of these waves looks to be very strong, but will still bring some gusty winds and precip of there own to most of the panhandle.

LONG TERM.../Thursday through Sunday/... Thursdays weather maker is currently an impressive hurricane force extratropical cyclone located near 44N 175W. This system will continue to travel east through the next few days but weaken as it moves into the Gulf, with the low center west of Dixon Entrance by Thursday morning. Overall confidence is high in the location of this system, with a wide range of pressure depth solutions; currently thinking the low will reach near 985mb by Thursday morning. As this system lifts north along the Alexander Archipelago coast expect outflow winds to start to diminish thru the Inner Channels, with another round of precipitation into Saturday morning. Currently not expecting any widespread snow impacts at sea level, warm air should have successfully infiltrated most areas across the Panhandle with the exception of Haines and Skagway highways. Look for a break in precipitation Sunday.

By the weekend, powerful swell from distant storms will continue to impact our coast; however, winds and fresh seas should be trending down. Look for our next large low to move into the Gulf by Monday or Tuesday of next week.

AVIATION.../Through 12z Wednesday/...The first of many fronts continues to move northward across the panhandle this morning. This front has now reached the northern panhandle bringing snow to areas from Juneau and Gustavus northward. Areas with snow have seen decreased VIS to AoB 6SM and CIGS to AoB 2500 ft. Lowest conditions are in PAHN this morning with VIS below 1 SM at times. Conditions in these areas will start to improve Tuesday morning as precipitation ends. Around the same time, about 18z, a second front will move northward into the southern panhandle bringing a second round of increased winds and precipitation. This front is looking very similar to the current departing system. The main difference is that it will be slightly warmer and keep snow to only far northern areas. That being said this, front will bring predominately VFR CIGS and VIS, but periods of MVFR are possible with CIGS just below 3000 ft and VIS around 4 to 6 SM. Increased wind and LLWS remain a concern for the far southern panhandle including PAKW and PAKT with the second front. Winds will once again begin to increase for those areas around 18z with gusts up to 35 to 40 kts possible into the afternoon.

MARINE... Inner Channels: Inner channels will be somewhat turbulent over the next few days as a series of fronts and troughs move through the panhandle from S to N. Wind directions in particular will be somewhat tricky especially over the central inner channels. The S inner channels will mainly stay out of the S direction with bursts of wind to 25 to 35 kt at times highest winds will likely be Tuesday late morning or midday. The N inner channels will mostly stay out of a N direction also with occasional burst of winds to 25 to 30 kt as the high in the Yukon remains strong enough to keep a N pressure gradient going through mid week. The central channels will be caught in the middle with periods of N winds followed by periods of S winds that flip back to the N as fronts pass through followed by the Yukon high reasserting itself. Wind speeds in the central channels could be as high as 25 kt at times as well from either direction. Seas will generally be wind wave to 5 to 6 ft, but higher seas to 9 ft near ocean entrances with a southern exposure could be encountered.

Eastern Gulf of Alaska: Gulf of AK waters feature a series of fronts and areas of low pressure moving from SE to NW through the area. The strongest of such is expected to ride up the outer coast Tuesday morning into Tuesday night with the low center staying around 90 to 100 miles offshore. Expect an area of min to moderate gale force winds around the low center that will travel SE to NW through the near shore waters of the eastern gulf on Tuesday. Otherwise most areas of the gulf will feature E to SE winds of 20 to 30 kt winds with occasional bursts to 35 kt near the stronger lows and troughs through mid week. Seas generally expected to be between 10 and 15 ft through mid week with a dominate SE swell of around 8 to 10 ft persisting into Thursday at least.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: By Monday, an active pattern will return with warm southwest flow aloft.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow in eastern Oregon early Wednesday.
- Wet, mild weather, with higher snow levels, over northern areas Thanksgiving Day. Cloudy but dry in southern areas.
- Rain and high-elevation snow in all areas Thursday night through Friday night, heaviest in Idaho north of the Snake Basin.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Satellite showed Weak warm front moving NE through our CWA this afternoon. Cold front along the coast and supporting upper trough will weaken moving inland tonight through Wednesday due to stronger upper ridge holding firm over the interior western US. Forecast has only a 15-25 percent chance of light rain and snow in Harney and Baker Counties overnight and early Wednesday, and even less in other zones. Also, patchy fog in the valleys during the night and morning hours. The next north Pacific storm looks stronger and wetter over the northern half of our CWA Thanksgiving Day, while the southern half should stay dry until Thursday night. Southern areas look wetter Thursday night, more so in Idaho than Oregon. Snow level, initially 4500 feet in ID to 5500 feet in OR, will rise to 6000 feet in ID to 8000 feet in OR Thanksgiving Day, highest in southern Harney County. Total estimated rainfall Wednesday evening through Friday .40 to .75 inch in northern areas, and less than .20 inch in the south, except .20 to .40 inch in southern mountains. Total estimated snowfall 3 to 6 inches, generally above pass levels. Temperatures will continue 5 to 10 degrees above normal.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: As an upper-level shortwave grazes our northern areas Friday and early Saturday, precipitation chances 30-60% will span lower elevations and 70-90% higher elevations (highest chances to the north). Snow levels will range 6000-8500 ft MSL with this round of precipitation, highest along the ID/NV and OR/NV borders. Wind speeds and gusts will increase overnight Friday into Saturday as this disturbance moves out of the area. Over the higher terrain of SW Idaho, gusts of 30-40 mph are currently forecast. High pressure will build into the region late Saturday into Sunday, bringing dry and mild conditions. Valley highs will be near 50 degrees through the weekend, generally 5 to 10 degrees above normal.

By Monday, an active pattern will return with warm southwest flow aloft. Models disagree on how far south Canadian cold air will track, with the current forecast favoring a return to near normal temperatures and snow levels lowering to 5500-6500 ft across the region through next Tuesday. Models remain aligned for the next week on a strong closed low moving into California-Nevada on Tuesday. The impact over the Intermountain West will depend on the track of the low. Several deterministic solutions favor the low positioned slightly further north, which would increase the precipitation forecast substantially by late Tuesday. Other solutions push this low and the moisture south, which would bring mostly dry conditions through the middle of the week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Things get more uncertain as we head into the weekend. Some model runs, namely the GFS/GEFS, favor a shallower trough, with the jet staying north of Colorado, while the ECMWF favors a deeper trough, with the jet placed over western Colorado.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A gradual warming trend likely through the rest of the week, with quiet weather expected through Thanksgiving.
- Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range on Friday.
- Next storm system could bring some snow to the region over the weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: With yesterday's shortwave moving off to the east and an upper-level ridge building behind it, conditions over the next couple of days will be fairly quiet weather-wise. Highs will be in the upper 40s/low 50s along the I-25 corridor and across the plains today and tomorrow, with the mountain valleys seeing highs in the upper 30s to low 40s. Thursday will see highs in the mid 50s for the urban corridor and plains, along with clear skies and light winds, making for a rather nice, sunny Thanksgiving. Friday should then cap off the week as our warmest day, as highs in the urban corridor/plains are expected to reach into the low 60s.

The upper-level ridge should also start to weaken on Friday, with the next system building to the north and west of Colorado. West/northwest flow aloft will start to strengthen, allowing for stronger winds (20-30mph sustained, 40-50mph gusts) along the northern Front Range. There's currently some uncertainty within the models regarding the exact timing of the strongest winds; the NBM has peak wind gusts occurring early Friday morning, between 5am-8am, while the deterministic GFS leans towards keeping any stronger gusts in the afternoon, between 12pm-6pm. Regardless, the strongest winds will occur at the mountain peaks and higher elevations, and with relative humidities expected to stay above 30% across the Front Range & foothills, fire weather shouldn't be much of a concern.

Things get more uncertain as we head into the weekend. Some model runs, namely the GFS/GEFS, favor a shallower trough, with the jet staying north of Colorado, while the ECMWF favors a deeper trough, with the jet placed over western Colorado. Additionally, the last several runs of the GFS have an initial weak shortwave move across the state Saturday into Sunday, followed by a deeper trough on Monday, while the ECMWF resolves only one system for the Saturday- Sunday time frame. A lot of this uncertainty comes from differences in how the models are handling the interactions of the upper-level ridge over the western U.S. with both a strong system over the eastern U.S. and a developing shortwave off the Pacific northwest. Ultimately, the timing of this system, and our precip chances over the weekend, will depend on what that low system to the east does, as well as how the shortwave to the northwest develops. Should the eastern system slow or stall over the Ohio Valley area, the ridge hanging over us would have nowhere to go, keeping things drier and warmer over the weekend. Similarly, if the shortwave dissipates before reaching us, as the GFS solution would suggest, our precip chances would be low. On the other hand, should that shortwave to the northwest strengthen and persist, as the ECMWF would suggest, we might be able to get some precip chances and cooler temperatures into the area.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Moving into Sunday and the start of next week we should briefly dry out with cooler temperatures on tap, warming back into Monday as another shortwave passes across the region.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Elevated winds are possible into this evening for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.
- Another round of even stronger and more widespread winds are possible Thursday into Friday.
- Forecast uncertainty in regards to precipitation remains high over the weekend due to notable model variance.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Tonight...Visible satellite imagery showing an interesting feature from Douglas, to Wheatland to Cheyenne. It looks like mountain wave clouds that are developing southwest to northeast, perpendicular to the flow aloft.

With a decent low and mid level height gradient under northwest flow aloft, we have been seeing gusts of 40 to 50 mph over our North Snowy Range Foothills along Interstate 80 including at Arlington, Foote Creek and Halleck Ridge. According to local wind models as well as the 850/700 mb Craig to Casper height gradients, expect these gusty winds to decrease later this afternoon and early this evening. Minimum temperatures will be tempered somewhat by the cloud cover and low level mixing.

Wednesday...Near perfect travel day in our neck of the woods before the Thanksgiving Holiday with the ridge aloft overhead and minimal wind. 700 mb temperatures near -1 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures in the 40s west of Interstate 25, with mid 40s to lower 50s further east.

Wednesday night...The ridge aloft is flattened somewhat by the next weak shortwave trough feature moving to the southeast across Wyoming, with no negligible weather effects noted. The airmass will moderate somewhat with low temperatures in the 20s at lower elevations and teens for the mountains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Continued uncertainty expected in the long term forecast due to model variance with differing amounts of precipitation possible, but no matter what a system will move through the region and bring strong winds with temperatures likely dropping as this moves through the region. Thursday into Friday the upper level transient ridge will continue it's progression through the region as it makes way for a strong Pacific trough and jet that will start to overtake by the end of the week. At the surface we'll see another dry and warm day for the Thanksgiving holiday with incoming cloudiness in response to the approaching system. On Friday upslope flow across the mountains increases, allowing wintry precipitation to resume for them. Winds meanwhile will ramp up late Thursday into Friday, and continue through Saturday before finally lessening, likely bringing a multi-day high wind event for our wind prone locations. Most guidance is in solid agreement on this already, with in-house models showing a 40-60% probability of high winds for the wind prones, and 850 mb pressure gradients of 60 to 80 meters, giving high confidence to the likelihood of this event.

What's less likely is precipitation outside of the mountains, with a wide swath of outcomes from all ensemble members. Everything from our usual dry conditions to Cheyenne seeing near 6 inches of snowfall is on the table. The higher precipitation chance scenarios also bring with them cooler temperatures, while the drier scenarios from the system just a bit further east bring warmer temperatures. As of this writing I would say ensembles seem to be favoring the lower elevations finally getting at least some meager precipitation, so hopefully Cheyenne will finally see it's first noteworthy accumulating snowfall this record setting year, but to what amount is still up in the air.

Moving into Sunday and the start of next week we should briefly dry out with cooler temperatures on tap, warming back into Monday as another shortwave passes across the region. This one will yet again feature the strongest forcing well to our south, so expect any precipitation to be limited once again to the mountains from orographic enhancement. Overall an active end to November, and hopefully we can finally achieve some precipitation for our incredibly dry eastern zones.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As the current ridge shifts eastward, deterministic guidance indicates a split flow pattern developing by Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry conditions on tap today and Wednesday.
- Patchy fog is possible in the lower valleys Wednesday morning as a result of clearing skies and high relative humidities.
- Active weather remains possible late this week, but some details remain uncertain at this time. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: MILD AND DRY CONDITIONS TODAY AND WEDNESDAY:

A fast moving ridge will begin to build into the area today in the wake of the previous system. This will cause generally mild and dry conditions for much of the region through Wednesday. Additionally, daytime highs for today and Wednesday will be hovering around normal for much of the region. Patchy fog could be a possibility again Wednesday morning in the lower valleys as overnight clearing skies in combination with high relative humidities will favor fog formation. There is a particularly strong signal for high relative humidities in the Uinta Basin area, but cloud cover will heavily dictate the fog that forms in that location.
ANOTHER SYSTEM EXPECTED AFTER THANKSGIVING:

As the current ridge shifts eastward, deterministic guidance indicates a split flow pattern developing by Thursday. A new ridge will build over Southern California, leaving our region sandwiched between a cutoff low to the south and stronger systems to our north and east. This setup will maintain generally dry conditions and above-normal temperatures through Thanksgiving. By Friday, the Southern California ridge will break down as the next system approaches. Resulting northwesterly flow will favor snowfall over the Park Range Friday and Saturday. Because model projections for snow totals continue to fluctuate daily, confidence in exact amounts remains low. However, anyone traveling late this week should prepare for potentially difficult conditions, especially across the northern mountains. Light impacts are also possible south of the Park Range, though confidence there is low as well. Please continue to monitor the forecast, as details will likely evolve over the coming days. Looking ahead to Sunday and early next week, models diverge on specific scenarios, though the overall pattern appears likely to remain unsettled.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: For next week, models continue to differ on timing and location of the expected wave train of Eastern Pacific systems translating across the CONUS, with NBM keeping main chances of precipitation along and west of the ContDvd, along with temperatures at to slightly above seasonal levels, with day to day changes likely, as said waves become more resolved.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A series of passing waves to bring chances of precipitation and cooler temperatures through the weekend and into early next week, though timing and location of each of these fast moving systems remains uncertain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis indicates moderating northwest flow aloft across the region, with yesterday's passing wave continuing to translate east across the Upper Midwest and High Plains, as upper level ridging builds across the Great Basin ahead of another Eastern Pacific system moving onshore across the Pacific Northwest Coast at this time. GOES satellite data has low clouds diminishing from west to east across the far southeast plains, with snow cover evident across the southern I-25 Corridor near Walsenburg, along with a small patch across central Kiowa county at this time.

With upper level ridging building across the region, dry conditions can be expected across the region tonight and through the day tomorrow. With dry air in place and clear skies overnight, lows will in be mainly in the teens and 20s areawide, with warming temperatures in the banana belt along and west of the I-25 early Wednesday morning, with weak lee troughing across the plains. Slight warming aloft will help warm temperatures back to around seasonal levels tomorrow, with highs in the 50s across the plains, and mainly in the 40s across the higher terrain under mostly sunny skies.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Latest model data continues to support the next Pacific system splitting as it moves across the Intermountain West and into the High Plains through Thursday night. This leaves the region in generally dry west to northwest flow through Thanksgiving night. This will also keep temperatures at and above seasonal levels through the period.

Increasing west to northwest flow remains expected across the region Friday ahead of more Eastern Pacific energy moving onshore across the Pacific Northwest. Breezy northwest winds will help boost temperatures well above seasonal levels into the 60s across the plains on Friday, with highs in the 40s and 50s across the higher terrain. This will also lead to heightened fire danger across the region on Friday.

For Saturday and Sunday, operational and ensemble model data continue to differ on the amplitude of said Pacific Northwest energy, with the latest EC and Canadian data being the further west digging the system across the Rockies on Saturday, which brings better chances of precipitation to eastern Colorado. Latest GFS data keeps the system further east, keeping precipitation mainly confined to the Northern and Central Mtns. NBM data seemingly splits the difference and has good chances of generally light snow across the Central Mountains on Saturday, as well as introduced slight chances of precipitation across the plains with a passing cold front. Temperatures look to remain above seasonal levels on Saturday, with dry weather and cooler temperatures in store areawide behind the passing system on Sunday.

For next week, models continue to differ on timing and location of the expected wave train of Eastern Pacific systems translating across the CONUS, with NBM keeping main chances of precipitation along and west of the ContDvd, along with temperatures at to slightly above seasonal levels, with day to day changes likely, as said waves become more resolved.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Late in the week, a shallow ridge will build into the southwestern US, resulting in largely zonal flow through the weekend and into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - High pressure will bring dry weather and near-seasonal temperatures across the area through Thanksgiving.
- A more mild airmass will spread across the region for the upcoming weekend, boosting temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal for late November.
- A weather system brushing by northern Utah late Friday will bring a chance of valley rain/mountain snow mainly north of I-80.

- A more active weather pattern will return next week as a series of weather systems pass through the region. This far out, considerable uncertainty remains regarding the timing and track of these systems.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Patchy fog was visible on satellite imagery earlier this morning, primarily limited to the Cache Valley and near area reservoirs (namely Deer Creek and Strawberry). Expect little change heading into tomorrow as a ridge of high pressure slowly passes overhead. A very weak, dry system will cross the area Wednesday night, but is unlikely to produce any impacts. Instead, valley inversions will likely strengthen, resulting in more valley haze along the Wasatch Front and a warming trend in the mountains.

Late in the week, a shallow ridge will build into the southwestern US, resulting in largely zonal flow through the weekend and into early next week. A couple of shortwave troughs will move through the mean flow, the first drawing moisture into northern Utah and southwest Wyoming late Friday into Saturday. Considerable uncertainty still remains in terms of QPF and snowfall, depending on exact flow direction and the southern extent of moisture into Utah. For example, the NBM 25th percentile for QPF between Friday and Saturday evening suggests only up to 0.15" in the northern mountains, whereas the 75th percentile suggests 0.50-1.00" of liquid equivalent. Another potential shortwave trough could cross the area late Sunday into Monday, but similar to the prior wave, plenty of uncertainty remains. Guidance does favor overall cyclonic flow next week across the western US, with more active weather looking more likely to return.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on slopes steeper than about 30 degrees at higher elevations. The most dangerous slopes are those with wind-drifted snow that face west to north through east. If you experience audible collapsing or shooting cracks, give suspect slopes a wide buffer and stick to lower-angle terrain, as you can trigger avalanches from a distance or from below.
Slopes less than 30 degrees in wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline offer safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Stiffer wind-drifted slopes on steep northwest to north to east-facing aspects are still dangerous and should be avoided. You can find these in isolated pockets in thinner areas, or they can be well connected in deeper snowpacks and triggered from a distance. By sticking to lower-angle, sheltered slopes, or more southerly aspects, you will lessen your odds of triggering a slide.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed isolated pockets of stiff snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe to travel on as there is very little snow. In the alpine, steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: In very isolated spots, you may find a drift of firm snow resting on old, weak snow. In steep terrain, steer clear of these areas to reduce avalanche risk. Unfortunately, these will also be the most attractive areas to ride.
